paras: The Fitzgerald church picnic shooting was a clash at a church picnic in Fitzgerald, Georgia, reported in August 1920, in which a crowd took a Black woman away from the white man accompanying her. The man drew a revolver and fired, and in what was described as a "near riot" one man was shot and several people were hurt. The episode is known from a single brief item in the Chicago Broad Ax.

According to the Broad Ax, a crowd at the picnic resented the appearance of a "colored woman" with a man the paper called her "white affinity." The crowd took "the girl" away from him, after which he pulled his revolver and began firing. One man was shot and several were hurt, though the item names no one and gives neither the race of the crowd nor that of the injured. The date of the picnic is not given, and no deaths were reported.
No report of arrests, charges or any official response appears in the coverage, and the condition of the wounded man is not stated.

The Chicago Broad Ax carried the story on its front page on August 21, 1920, under the headline "Object to White Man With Colored Woman at Picnic." The item ran as a single datelined sentence without comment, and its headline cast the clash as an objection to a white man appearing with a Black woman. No account in white newspapers, Georgia papers or other Black papers was found.
